passages.text: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. It has matched or outperformed AdamW in language-model pretraining, from speedrun benchmarks ( Jordan et al., 2024a ) to large-scale training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , and standard optimizers more broadly in vision ( Jordan et al., 2024b ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) , diffusion ( Schaipp, 2025 ) , and tabular models ( Gorishniy et al., 2026 ) . The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015a ; Carlson et al., 2016 ; Carlson et al., 2015b ) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) . It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . Controlled benchmarks place such matrix-based optimizers among the strongest available ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , so understanding when a step along polar ⁡ ( G ) \mathrm{polar}(G) helps matters well beyond Muon .

Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) .

• Implicit preconditioning (Section 4 ). PolarGD is a gradient step with a preconditioner set by the current iterate, whose condition number is that of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. When the iterate has full row rank, this gives an exact formula for the progress per step, for line search and fixed steps. PolarGD is therefore fastest when the rows of X k X_{k} are orthogonal with equal norms and slowest when X k X_{k} has tiny singular values; this slow regime is tight, and in it GD can be nearly one-step exact while PolarGD stays slow along the trajectory. We also show that a direction that is better for one step need not give a faster trajectory. • Rank deficiency and finite Newton--Schulz (Section 4.2 ). We extend these identities to rank-deficient iterates and show that a few Newton--Schulz steps, as used in Muon , give a softened polar update: they behave like damped polar, treating large singular values like exact polar and tiny ones like a GD step. Near rank deficiency this converges faster than exact polar, so finite Newton--Schulz is not merely an approximation of the polar factor.

We isolated the geometry of the orthogonalized update shared by Muon and related matrix optimizers by analyzing PolarGD on matrix quadratics. PolarGD benefits from orthogonal equivariance and implicit preconditioning by the iterate, but it is not uniformly better than GD or SignGD : it is fast near row-isotropic iterates and slow near rank deficiency, where exact polar normalization overweights tiny singular values. Finite Newton--Schulz softens the update exactly there and can then converge faster than exact polar, so it is not merely an approximation of the polar factor. The trajectory results rely on the quadratic structure, but Proposition 1 only needs the curvature bounds ( 2 ), and equivariance and the softening by Newton--Schulz hold for any objective, including the momentum matrix that Muon orthogonalizes. Our transformer measurements show that the regime where exact polar and Newton--Schulz differ occurs in practice. This suggests treating the number of Newton--Schulz steps, or the damping level, as a design choice of the optimizer rather than only as an accuracy setting.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories like Hugging Face host many such LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept, character, style, or task. Users routinely want to combine several LoRAs in a single generation, but two existing strategies involve a trade-off with each other. First, combining the LoRA weights into a single update before inference (e.g., static merge) needs only one forward pass, but quality drops, because LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere when their weights are summed into a single update, distorting each LoRA’s contribution. Second, running each LoRA in a separate forward pass and summing the outputs (e.g., composite) preserves output quality, but each LoRA adds a full backbone pass, so inference time scales linearly with the active LoRA count. To recover composite-level quality at merge cost, we study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that preserves 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the sum of individual LoRA ranks is enough to represent the pool, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 NLP tasks shows comparable overlap (about 62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline at 96%, indicating that across these five pools pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We use this overlap to construct LoRASpace , a training-free pool-wide method where the subspace matrices are computed once per pool and reused

ather than modality predicts where compression is large. We use this overlap to construct LoRASpace , a training-free pool-wide method where the subspace matrices are computed once per pool and reused across two inference modes: a static mode at merge inference cost, and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing at substantially lower cost than composite. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace achieves more than 6 × 6\times speedup over composite at six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mostly by running one backbone pass instead of six. In our ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace , so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, the framework predicts limited compression benefit, with gains coming from external retrieval coupling. Code is available at https://github.com/Thamirawaran/loraspace .

Two ambient strategies have emerged for this multi-LoRA problem. The first, static merge ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) , folds the chosen LoRAs into a single weight update ( delta for short) before inference, so only one forward pass is required. Static merge is cheap to deploy but tends to lose individual LoRA identity, since unrelated low-rank directions are summed in the ambient parameter space. The second strategy, often called composite ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) , runs one forward pass per active LoRA and aggregates the outputs. Composite preserves quality more faithfully but pays linearly in compute and memory with the number of active LoRAs. On modern diffusion backbones, this can mean several minutes per image at high LoRA counts, with proportional cost growth on language models. The two strategies sit at opposite corners of a quality-cost trade-off because both treat each LoRA as an independent low-rank addition in ambient space.

We observe that both the merge and composite views ignore a structural property of real LoRA pools. When the per-LoRA factors of a pool are stacked and decomposed jointly, the resulting subspace is much smaller than the sum of individual ranks. On language LoRAs trained on related tasks this reflects alignment between adapters, while on diffusion pools it comes largely from layer-width saturation and each adapter’s own spectral tail (§ 4.2 ). We capture this with the rank-fill ratio ρ = D / ∑ i r i \rho=D/\sum_{i}r_{i} , where D D is the rank-truncated subspace dimension obtained by an energy-truncated SVD of the stacked factors, and ∑ i r i \sum_{i}r_{i} is the no-overlap upper bound. Based on this overlap, we introduce LoRASpace , a training-free composition operator whose goal is to recover composite-level quality at near-merge inference cost while supporting input-dependent routing, built from a rank-truncated pool-wide substrate ( U , V ) (U,V) computed once at pool-creation time and reused for any active subset of LoRAs chosen at inference. The substrate supports two deployment modes from one cache. A static mode folds time-invariant routing into a single combined delta at ambient-merge inference cost. A dynamic mode accepts context-dependent routing through a router function { w i } \{w_{i}\} that maps the current generation context (token, step, pixel, or prompt) to per-LoRA weights, at substantially lower cost than composite. On diffusion pools, LoRASpace matches or exceeds composite quality at merge cost ( + 0.74 +0.74 CLIP-T on Pool A) and reaches 6.1 × 6.1\times speedup over composite at high LoRA counts, mostly by running one backbone pass instead of one per LoRA. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever LLM benchmark, the framework predicts no compression

On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever LLM benchmark, the framework predicts no compression speedup, and accuracy gains over ambient mixture come from pairing the substrate with external retrieval ( + 0.96 +0.96 Macro Task).

We organise the evaluation around four findings: rank-fill regime characterisation across diffusion and LLM pools (§ 4.2 ); a quality + mechanism comparison showing static-mode LoRASpace delivers composite-level quality at ambient-merge cost and that the lift is rank- D D truncation in any basis (§ 4.3 ); robustness to the energy truncation threshold (§ 4.4 ); and a routing ablation showing router quality varies on Pool A (temporal helps, semantic is flat, spatial regresses on ImageReward; § 4.5 ). passages.text: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches , causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss , a property we denote as KV-shareability . However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model’s quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning’s unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice! , we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8 , mxfp8 , nvfp4 ). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

In this section, we study KV-shareability in looped architectures. To evaluate KV-shareability, we compare shared evaluations , which reuse the final-recurrence cache across all recurrences, against unshared evaluations , which retain every recurrence’s cache. Details on reproducing accurate KV-sharing inference setups for our benchmarks are provided in Appendix C . We motivate our investigation by observing that KV-shareability is not universal to all looped models (see Table 1 ). We establish that stochastic depth enables contractive recurrent dynamics, which we formally analyze and empirically validate allows KV-shareability when fixed points agree under shared and unshared KV-caches ( Section 3.1 ). However, stochastic depth alone is insufficient to guarantee agreement, leading to models not exhibiting KV-shareability (e.g., Parcae 1.3B in Table 1 ). Analyzing failure cases, we find that KV-sharing creates a token-independent basis shift, causing convergence to different fixed points and degraded quality under KV-sharing ( Section 3.2 ).

For long-context memory experiments, we implement efficient KV-sharing for Parcae [ 50 ] in sglang [ 77 ] . We report total GPU memory usage, including model weights, KV-cache storage, CUDA graphs, and runtime buffers. For workload experiments, we replay production-derived Mooncake requests [ 51 ] using AIPerf [ 46 ] , preserving arrival times, input/output lengths, and prefix-sharing relations. To study realistic model scales, we construct proxy models from standard open-weights (e.g., GLM 4.7-FP8 [ 64 ] ) by repeatedly looping the middle third transformer blocks, with and without KV-sharing. We vary both the offered request rate and maximum concurrency to characterize performance across load- and concurrency-limited regimes, respectively.

In Figure 9 , we observe that memory savings scale with recurrence count ( μ rec \mu_{\text{rec}} ) and KV-cache size. At μ rec = 8 \mu_{\text{rec}}=8 , KV-sharing increases the total token capacity to 3.33 × 3.33\times the unshared capacity under the same KV-memory budget. passages.text: Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum ( HyM ), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients’ iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON , which applies Newton–Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon.

passages.text: Muon orthogonalizes a weight matrix’s momentum before each step, and on neural networks this simple preconditioner beats AdamW in a wide range of tasks. passages.text: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00% over this baseline.

In this section, we present the main comparison results by applying NormTune to representative PEFT methods, including LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, and evaluating their effectiveness for test-time scaling. As shown in Table 1 , rank-8 PEFT methods underperform on reasoning-intensive tasks. Incorporating NormTune substantially improves their performance, yielding average gains of 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% for LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, respectively. Rank-8 NormTune-enhanced PEFT surpasses 90% of full fine-tuning performance and consistently outperform AdaLoRA, LoRA+, rsLoRA, DoRA and TempBalance+PEFT under the same rank-8 setting. When increasing the rank to 256, NormTune still brings consistent improvements to PEFT methods, with average gains of 13.44%, 10.46%, and 9.77% for LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, respectively. Notably, all three NormTune-enhanced variants surpass S1 (Full-FT) by 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00%, respectively. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we further compare NormTune with state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning-based reasoning models. Using the same Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct backbone, all NormTune-enhanced variants outperform T1 (Qwen2.5-32B), and NormTune+MoRA further surpasses SSFT-32B-GFPO by 0.58%. These results show that NormTune substantially improves model performance with lower resource consumption.

For Z1-7B based one Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, we further evaluate code-related reasoning performance, as shown in Table 2 . Under supervised fine-tuning with a similar model size, NormTune+LoRA, NormTune+Bone, and NormTune+MoRA all achieve performance comparable to the state-of-the-art full fine-tuning baseline Z1-7B (Full-FT). Notably, NormTune+LoRA further surpasses Z1-7B by over 0.6%. For RL-based training, NormTune+LoRA also achieves a performance level comparable to GPT-4o-0513, with an average score of 46.0 versus 47.7. This demonstrates the effectiveness of NormTune across various testing datasets. For OLMo-3-7B, as shown in Table 3 , all NormTune-enhanced methods, including NormTune+LoRA, NormTune+Bone, and NormTune+MoRA, outperform Full-FT. These results show that NormTune remains effective even for smaller models. Qwen3-4B experiments are presented in the Appendix in Table 7 . Across scales from 4B to 32B and across mathematical reasoning, code reasoning, and scientific question-answering benchmarks, NormTune consistently improves different PEFT methods. This demonstrates that NormTune is a general and scalable solution for improving test-time scaling with strong performance.

We further evaluate NormTune on Qwen3-4B across GPQA, AIME’24, and AIME’25 benchmarks. As shown in Table 7 , NormTune consistently improves different PEFT backbones across model families and reasoning benchmarks. On Qwen3-4B, NormTune+LoRA improves the average score from 37.7% to 44.2%, surpassing Full-FT by 6%, while NormTune+MoRA improves MoRA from 33.9% to 42.9%. passages.text: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories like Hugging Face host many such LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept, character, style, or task. Users routinely want to combine several LoRAs in a single generation, but two existing strategies involve a trade-off with each other. First, combining the LoRA weights into a single update before inference (e.g., static merge) needs only one forward pass, but quality drops, because LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere when their weights are summed into a single update, distorting each LoRA’s contribution. Second, running each LoRA in a separate forward pass and summing the outputs (e.g., composite) preserves output quality, but each LoRA adds a full backbone pass, so inference time scales linearly with the active LoRA count. To recover composite-level quality at merge cost, we study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that preserves 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the sum of individual LoRA ranks is enough to represent the pool, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 NLP tasks shows comparable overlap (about 62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline at 96%, indicating that across these five pools pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We use this overlap to construct LoRASpace , a training-free pool-wide method where the subspace matrices are computed once per pool and reused

We use this overlap to construct LoRASpace , a training-free pool-wide method where the subspace matrices are computed once per pool and reused across two inference modes: a static mode at merge inference cost, and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing at substantially lower cost than composite. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace achieves more than 6 × 6\times speedup over composite at six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mostly by running one backbone pass instead of six. In our ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace , so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, the framework predicts limited compression benefit, with gains coming from external retrieval coupling. Code is available at https://github.com/Thamirawaran/loraspace .

Two ambient strategies have emerged for this multi-LoRA problem. The first, static merge ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) , folds the chosen LoRAs into a single weight update ( delta for short) before inference, so only one forward pass is required. Static merge is cheap to deploy but tends to lose individual LoRA identity, since unrelated low-rank directions are summed in the ambient parameter space. The second strategy, often called composite ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) , runs one forward pass per active LoRA and aggregates the outputs. Composite preserves quality more faithfully but pays linearly in compute and memory with the number of active LoRAs. On modern diffusion backbones, this can mean several minutes per image at high LoRA counts, with proportional cost growth on language models. The two strategies sit at opposite corners of a quality-cost trade-off because both treat each LoRA as an independent low-rank addition in ambient space.

We observe that both the merge and composite views ignore a structural property of real LoRA pools. When the per-LoRA factors of a pool are stacked and decomposed jointly, the resulting subspace is much smaller than the sum of individual ranks. On language LoRAs trained on related tasks this reflects alignment between adapters, while on diffusion pools it comes largely from layer-width saturation and each adapter’s own spectral tail (§ 4.2 ). We capture this with the rank-fill ratio ρ = D / ∑ i r i \rho=D/\sum_{i}r_{i} , where D D is the rank-truncated subspace dimension obtained by an energy-truncated SVD of the stacked factors, and ∑ i r i \sum_{i}r_{i} is the no-overlap upper bound. passages.text: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches , causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss , a property we denote as KV-shareability . However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model’s quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning’s unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice! , we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8 , mxfp8 , nvfp4 ). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

In this section, we study KV-shareability in looped architectures. To evaluate KV-shareability, we compare shared evaluations , which reuse the final-recurrence cache across all recurrences, against unshared evaluations , which retain every recurrence’s cache. Details on reproducing accurate KV-sharing inference setups for our benchmarks are provided in Appendix C . We motivate our investigation by observing that KV-shareability is not universal to all looped models (see Table 1 ). We establish that stochastic depth enables contractive recurrent dynamics, which we formally analyze and empirically validate allows KV-shareability when fixed points agree under shared and unshared KV-caches ( Section 3.1 ). However, stochastic depth alone is insufficient to guarantee agreement, leading to models not exhibiting KV-shareability (e.g., Parcae 1.3B in Table 1 ). Analyzing failure cases, we find that KV-sharing creates a token-independent basis shift, causing convergence to different fixed points and degraded quality under KV-sharing ( Section 3.2 ).

For long-context memory experiments, we implement efficient KV-sharing for Parcae [ 50 ] in sglang [ 77 ] . We report total GPU memory usage, including model weights, KV-cache storage, CUDA graphs, and runtime buffers. To study realistic model scales, we construct proxy models from standard open-weights (e.g., GLM 4.7-FP8 [ 64 ] ) by repeatedly looping the middle third transformer blocks, with and without KV-sharing. passages.text: Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum ( HyM ), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients’ iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON , which applies Newton–Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon.

passages.text: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00% over this baseline.

In this section, we present the main comparison results by applying NormTune to representative PEFT methods, including LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, and evaluating their effectiveness for test-time scaling. As shown in Table 1 , rank-8 PEFT methods underperform on reasoning-intensive tasks. Incorporating NormTune substantially improves their performance, yielding average gains of 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% for LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, respectively. Rank-8 NormTune-enhanced PEFT surpasses 90% of full fine-tuning performance and consistently outperform AdaLoRA, LoRA+, rsLoRA, DoRA and TempBalance+PEFT under the same rank-8 setting. When increasing the rank to 256, NormTune still brings consistent improvements to PEFT methods, with average gains of 13.44%, 10.46%, and 9.77% for LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, respectively. Notably, all three NormTune-enhanced variants surpass S1 (Full-FT) by 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00%, respectively. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we further compare NormTune with state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning-based reasoning models. Using the same Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct backbone, all NormTune-enhanced variants outperform T1 (Qwen2.5-32B), and NormTune+MoRA further surpasses SSFT-32B-GFPO by 0.58%. These results show that NormTune substantially improves model performance with lower resource consumption.

For Z1-7B based one Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, we further evaluate code-related reasoning performance, as shown in Table 2 . Under supervised fine-tuning with a similar model size, NormTune+LoRA, NormTune+Bone, and NormTune+MoRA all achieve performance comparable to the state-of-the-art full fine-tuning baseline Z1-7B (Full-FT). Notably, NormTune+LoRA further surpasses Z1-7B by over 0.6%. For RL-based training, NormTune+LoRA also achieves a performance level comparable to GPT-4o-0513, with an average score of 46.0 versus 47.7. This demonstrates the effectiveness of NormTune across various testing datasets. For OLMo-3-7B, as shown in Table 3 , all NormTune-enhanced methods, including NormTune+LoRA, NormTune+Bone, and NormTune+MoRA, outperform Full-FT. These results show that NormTune remains effective even for smaller models. Qwen3-4B experiments are presented in the Appendix in Table 7 . Across scales from 4B to 32B and across mathematical reasoning, code reasoning, and scientific question-answering benchmarks, NormTune consistently improves different PEFT methods. This demonstrates that NormTune is a general and scalable solution for improving test-time scaling with strong performance.

We further evaluate NormTune on Qwen3-4B across GPQA, AIME’24, and AIME’25 benchmarks. As shown in Table 7 , NormTune consistently improves different PEFT backbones across model families and reasoning benchmarks. On Qwen3-4B, NormTune+LoRA improves the average score from 37.7% to 44.2%, surpassing Full-FT by 6%, while NormTune+MoRA improves MoRA from 33.9% to 42.9%. NormTune+Bone also achieves consistent gains and reaches performance comparable to Full-FT. However, TempBalance+LoRA, TempBalance+Bone, and TempBalance+MoRA reduced performance by 0.7%, 11%, and 17.3% compared with LoRA, Bone, and MoRA, respectively.
